clinicalPearls: An apocrine hidrocystoma is a benign cystic lesion arising from the apocrine glands of Moll at the eyelid margin, presenting as a smooth, dome-shaped, translucent cyst.
It is characteristically solitary and often has a bluish or bluish-black translucent hue owing to the Tyndall effect of clear fluid within the cyst, and it transilluminates.
The lesion is filled with clear or slightly milky fluid and, unlike an eccrine hidrocystoma, does not enlarge specifically with heat or sweating.
It is typically found at or near the lid margin, most often the inner or outer canthus, and is usually asymptomatic apart from cosmetic concern.
Diagnosis is clinical; transillumination helps confirm the cystic, fluid-filled nature and distinguish it from a solid or pigmented lesion.
Definitive treatment is complete surgical excision including the cyst wall; simple puncture or incision leads to recurrence because the secretory lining persists.
A bluish eyelid-margin lesion must be differentiated from pigmented lesions such as naevus or melanoma, and from a nodular basal cell carcinoma, so atypical lesions warrant histology.
Multiple apocrine or eccrine hidrocystomas can occur and, when numerous, may be associated with ectodermal dysplasia syndromes such as Schopf-Schulz-Passarge and Goltz syndromes.
reference.pathophysiology: Apocrine hidrocystomas are adenomatous cystic proliferations (cystadenomas) derived from the apocrine secretory glands of Moll in the eyelid margin, rather than simple retention cysts. The cyst is lined by an inner layer of columnar secretory epithelium showing decapitation (apocrine) secretion and an outer layer of myoepithelial cells, and papillary projections may extend into the lumen. Active apocrine secretion fills the cavity with proteinaceous fluid; the overlying thin wall and clear contents scatter light to give the characteristic translucent bluish appearance. Because the lesion is a true secretory neoplasm with a retained lining, incomplete removal allows continued secretion and recurrence.
additionalDifferentials: Melanocytic naevus of the eyelid margin
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination of the lid margin to characterise the cyst
Transillumination to confirm the fluid-filled cystic nature
Dermoscopy to distinguish from pigmented and vascular lesions
External photography for documentation and monitoring
Excisional biopsy with histopathology to confirm diagnosis and exclude malignancy in atypical lesions
Assessment for associated features of ectodermal dysplasia when lesions are multiple
redFlags: Irregular pigmentation, ulceration or induration suggesting melanoma or basal cell carcinoma
Rapid growth or recurrence after excision
A solid rather than transilluminating lesion, casting doubt on the cystic diagnosis
Multiple lesions prompting evaluation for an underlying ectodermal dysplasia syndrome
reference.prognosis: Benign with an excellent prognosis; complete excision including the cyst wall is curative. Recurrence follows incomplete removal, and multiple lesions may recur individually.
pitfalls: Treating by simple incision or drainage, which leaves the secretory lining and leads to recurrence
Mistaking a bluish translucent cyst for a pigmented naevus or melanoma, or vice versa
Failing to excise the full cyst wall at the lid margin, risking recurrence or marginal notching
Overlooking an associated ectodermal dysplasia syndrome in patients with numerous lesions
Not obtaining histology when the lesion has atypical or solid features
